final_answer:
Ice floats on water due to the unique molecular structure of water. Water molecules are polar, meaning they have a slight positive charge on one end and a slight negative charge on the other. This polarity allows water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with each other. 

When water freezes, the molecules arrange themselves into a hexagonal lattice structure. This structure is more open and spaced out compared to the more compact arrangement of molecules in liquid water. As a result, ice is less dense than liquid water, which causes it to float. This unusual property is crucial for the survival of aquatic life in cold climates, as it allows ice to form on the surface of lakes and rivers, insulating the water below.
